title: Babylon and the Land of Israel
bigQuestion: How did rabbis in two faraway lands turn the short Mishnah into the long Talmud?

story.title: A Question Crosses the Desert
story.kicker: A question asked by a lake in Tiberias finds its answer in Babylon, three generations later.
paragraphs: The sun is warm on the Sea of Galilee. In the town of Tiberias, around the year 250, a student reads a line of the Mishnah out loud. It is a rule about a lost coat. He stops. "But what if the coat has no mark on it?" he asks. His teacher, Rabbi Yochanan, nods. "Good question," he says. "I am not sure. Let us keep it."

The question does not stay in Tiberias. A traveler named Rav Dimi is packing for a long trip. He is going east to Babylon, where many Jews live. He carries no books. He carries teachings in his memory. He has learned this question by heart, along with dozens of others. Then he walks with a caravan for many weeks.

In Babylon, the rabbis meet in a big hall near a river. Rav Dimi tells them what the teachers in the Land of Israel said. Some agree. Some do not. One rabbi finds a verse from the Torah that helps. Another finds an old teaching that seems to say the opposite. They argue all afternoon. They do not finish. The question is passed to their students.

Years go by. Then more years. Rabbis who were babies when the question was first asked are now old men with white beards. In a school called Pumbedita, a teacher finally gives an answer that most of the others accept. He explains his reason step by step. His answer is remembered. Much later it is written down right beside the question.

This is how the Gemara was made. Not by one person in one place, but by many rabbis in two lands, over about three hundred years. A question in one town, an answer in another, and every step in between kept on the page. When you open the Talmud today, you can still hear them talking.
story.think: Why do you think the rabbis kept the whole argument on the page, and not just the final answer?

lessons.title: After the Mishnah
lessons.mainIdea: The Gemara is the rabbis' long discussion of the Mishnah, and Mishnah plus Gemara equals Talmud.
reading: Around the year 200, Rabbi Judah the Prince finished the Mishnah. It was short and clear. But short rules make people ask questions. What does this word mean? What if two rules seem to disagree? Why did the Mishnah say it this way? Rabbis in the Land of Israel and in Babylon began to study it line by line.

The rabbis' discussion of the Mishnah is called the *Gemara*. The word comes from Aramaic and means something like "completion" or "study." The rabbis of the Gemara are called *amoraim*. One of them is an *amora*, which means "one who speaks" or "one who explains." They lived from about 200 to about 500 CE.

Put the two parts together and you get the *Talmud*. Talmud means "learning." A page of Talmud shows a line of Mishnah, then the Gemara that talks about it. The Gemara does not just give an answer. It shows the question, the proof, the objection and the reply, so a reader can follow the whole path.

words.d: the rabbis' discussion of the Mishnah, written mostly in Aramaic between about 200 and 500 CE
a rabbi of the Gemara (about 200 to 500 CE); the plural is amoraim
the Mishnah together with the Gemara; the word means "learning"

look.title: One Line, Then a Question
look.text: Mishnah: If you find a lost coat, announce it so the owner can claim it. Gemara: How long must the finder keep announcing it? What if the coat has no special mark? What if the owner has already given up hope of finding it? The rabbis take each question in turn.
look.prompt: Which of the Gemara's three questions would you ask first, and why?

check.q: What is the Gemara?
choices: The rabbis' discussion of the Mishnah
The first five books of the Bible
A short list of rules written by Judah the Prince
A prayer said in the evening
check.why: The Gemara is the long discussion of the Mishnah by the rabbis of about 200 to 500 CE.

check.q: What do you get when you put the Mishnah and the Gemara together?
check.why: Mishnah plus Gemara equals Talmud, a word that means "learning."

check.q: What is an amora?
check.why: An amora is a rabbi of the Gemara; the rabbis of the Mishnah are called tannaim.

lessons.title: The Land of Israel
lessons.mainIdea: In the Land of Israel, rabbis in Galilee towns like Tiberias studied the Mishnah under Roman rule.
reading: The Mishnah was finished in the Land of Israel, in the north, in a hilly region called *Galilee*. Rome ruled the land. Many rabbis lived in the towns of Sepphoris, Caesarea and *Tiberias*, a town on the shore of the Sea of Galilee. Tiberias became the most important center for study after about 250.

The best-known teacher there was Rabbi Yochanan. Historians think he died around 279 CE. His study partner was Resh Lakish. The Talmud says Resh Lakish had once been a strong man who lived by his sword, and Rabbi Yochanan talked him into a life of study. The two argued about almost every line.

Rabbi Yochanan valued his partner's objections. The Talmud tells that after Resh Lakish died, other students only agreed with the teacher, and this made him sad. A good study partner pushes back. The rabbis of the Land of Israel wrote their Gemara in their own kind of Aramaic, with plenty of Hebrew mixed in.

words.d: the hilly northern part of the Land of Israel, where the rabbis of the Mishnah and the Jerusalem Talmud mostly lived
a town on the Sea of Galilee that became the main center for rabbis in the Land of Israel

look.title: A Partner Who Pushed Back
look.text: The Gemara tells that after Resh Lakish died, a new student was sent to study with Rabbi Yochanan. The student kept agreeing with him. Rabbi Yochanan said that Resh Lakish used to raise twenty-four objections to each thing he said, and answering them made the teaching clear. Agreement, he said, did not help him learn.
look.cite: Babylonian Talmud, Bava Metzia 84a, retold in plain words from the William Davidson Talmud (Sefaria, 2017)
look.prompt: Why did Rabbi Yochanan miss being argued with? What did the objections do for him?

check.q: Which town became the main study center in the Land of Israel after about 250?
check.why: Tiberias, on the Sea of Galilee, was where Rabbi Yochanan and many other rabbis taught.

check.q: Who was Rabbi Yochanan's study partner?
check.why: Resh Lakish argued with Rabbi Yochanan about almost every line, and Rabbi Yochanan valued it.

check.q: Who ruled the Land of Israel in the time of the amoraim?
check.why: Rome ruled the Land of Israel; Persia ruled Babylon, the other center of study.

lessons.title: Babylon, Today's Iraq
lessons.mainIdea: A large Jewish community had lived in Babylon since the exile, and it became the Talmud's other home.
reading: Far to the east of the Land of Israel lay *Babylonia*, between the Tigris and Euphrates rivers. Today that land is Iraq. Jews had lived there for a very long time. In 586 BCE the Babylonians destroyed the First Temple and carried many people from Judah into exile. Some went home later. Many stayed.

By the time of the Mishnah, Babylonia was a large and settled Jewish community. Farmers grew dates and grain. Traders sailed the rivers. The rulers were Persian kings, called the Sasanians from about 224 CE. The Persians let the Jewish community run many of its own affairs.

The community had a leader called the *Exilarch*, the "head of the exile." Jewish tradition says his family came from King David. The Exilarch dealt with the Persian court and helped support the schools. In these schools the rabbis of Babylon studied the Mishnah that had come from the west.

words.d: the land between the Tigris and Euphrates rivers, today Iraq, home to a large Jewish community
the leader of the Jews in Babylonia, who spoke for the community to the Persian kings

look.title: Remembering Zion by the River
look.text: By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat down, yea, we wept, when we remembered Zion.
look.prompt: This psalm is about the first exiles, long before the Talmud. What does it tell you about how the Jews of Babylon remembered the Land of Israel?

check.q: Which country today covers the land the rabbis called Babylonia?
check.why: Babylonia lay between the Tigris and Euphrates rivers, in what is now Iraq.

check.q: Who was the Exilarch?
choices: The leader of the Jews in Babylonia
check.why: The Exilarch, or "head of the exile," led the Jewish community in Babylonia and spoke to the Persian court.

check.q: Why were there so many Jews in Babylonia?
choices: Many stayed after the exile of 586 BCE
They moved there to study with Rashi
check.why: Babylon destroyed the First Temple in 586 BCE and carried people into exile; many families stayed for centuries.

lessons.title: Sura and Rav
lessons.mainIdea: Rav brought the Mishnah to Babylon and founded the academy at Sura, where Talmud study began there.
reading: Tradition says a teacher called Rav had studied with Judah the Prince in the Land of Israel. Around 219 CE he traveled east to Babylonia. He brought the Mishnah with him, in his memory. He settled in a town called *Sura* and started a school. A school like this is called an *academy*.

Another great teacher, Shmuel, led the school at Nehardea. Tradition remembers him as a doctor who also knew the stars. Rav and Shmuel disagreed often. The Gemara records both opinions. A later rule says: in matters of ritual, follow Rav; in matters of money, follow Shmuel.

Sura lasted for hundreds of years. Rav Ashi taught there much later, around 400. The academies of Babylonia did not look like a school today. Students sat in rows by rank. The head of the academy sat in front. A speaker repeated his words loudly so everyone could hear. Then the arguing began.

words.d: a town in Babylonia where Rav founded an academy around 219 CE
a school where rabbis and students studied and argued about the Mishnah; in Hebrew, yeshiva

look.title: When Two Teachers Disagree
look.text: The Gemara states a rule for the many disagreements between Rav and Shmuel. When the question is about ritual, such as what is permitted or forbidden, the law follows Rav. When the question is about money, such as who owes what, the law follows Shmuel.
look.cite: Babylonian Talmud, Bekhorot 49b, retold in plain words from the William Davidson Talmud (Sefaria, 2017)
look.prompt: Why might it help to have a rule for deciding between two teachers, instead of picking one teacher for everything?

check.q: Who founded the academy at Sura?
check.why: Rav, who had studied with Judah the Prince, went to Babylonia around 219 CE and founded the school at Sura.

check.q: In the disagreements of Rav and Shmuel, whose view is followed in questions about money?
check.why: Bekhorot 49b says the law follows Shmuel in matters of money and Rav in matters of ritual.

check.q: What is an academy in this course?
choices: A palace of the Persian king
A school where rabbis studied and argued
check.why: An academy, or yeshiva, was a school where rabbis and students studied the Mishnah together.

lessons.title: Pumbedita, Abaye and Rava
lessons.mainIdea: At Pumbedita, Abaye and Rava argued so well that later readers called all Talmud study "the debates of Abaye and Rava."
reading: In 259 CE the town of Nehardea was destroyed in a war. Its scholars moved. A new academy grew up at *Pumbedita*, on the Euphrates river. For centuries Sura and Pumbedita were the two great schools of Babylonia. Students called them simply "the two academies."

The most famous pair from Pumbedita were Abaye and Rava. They lived in the 300s CE. They had studied together as young men. Then they argued for the rest of their lives. The Gemara records their debates on hundreds of pages. In most of them, later readers follow Rava's view. But Abaye's side is always kept.

Twice a year, in the months of Adar and Elul, the academies held a *kallah*. Farmers and traders left their work and came to study for a whole month. They reviewed one tractate together. Then they went home. The Talmud was never only for rabbis. It was for anyone who came.

words.d: an academy on the Euphrates river in Babylonia, famous for Abaye and Rava
a study month held twice a year, when farmers and traders came to the academy to learn a tractate

look.title: The Hall in a Kallah Month
look.text: Picture a long hall in Pumbedita in the month of Elul. The head of the academy sits in front. Rows of scholars sit by rank. Behind them sit farmers who have left their date palms, and traders who have tied up their boats. A speaker repeats each line so the back rows can hear. Someone in row twelve raises a hand with a question.
look.prompt: What might it feel like to be a farmer in row twelve, asking a question in front of the great scholars?

check.q: Which two teachers of Pumbedita are the most famous pair of the Gemara?
check.why: Abaye and Rava, who lived in the 300s CE, argued on hundreds of pages of the Gemara.

check.q: What was a kallah month?
choices: A month when farmers and traders came to study at the academy
A month when the Talmud was printed
check.why: In Adar and Elul, working people came to the academy for a month to review a tractate together.

check.q: What happened to Nehardea in 259 CE?
choices: It became the capital of Persia
It was destroyed in a war
check.why: Nehardea was destroyed in 259 CE; its scholars moved, and Pumbedita rose in its place.

lessons.title: Travelers With Good Memories
lessons.mainIdea: Travelers carried teachings between the Land of Israel and Babylon, so the two centers kept answering each other.
reading: There were no phones and no printing presses. So how did the rabbis of Tiberias know what was said in Sura? People walked. Some rabbis made the long journey again and again. They learned teachings by heart in one land and repeated them in the other. The Gemara often says, "When Rav Dimi came, he said..."

Rav Dimi and a scholar named Ulla were two of these travelers. Their trips took weeks each way. Because of them, an answer given in Babylon could be tested in Galilee, and a ruling from Galilee could be argued over in Pumbedita. The two Gemaras grew apart, but they never stopped talking.

Both centers spoke *Aramaic*, the everyday language of the Middle East then. But each had its own kind. Babylonian Aramaic and the Aramaic of Galilee sounded a little different, like English in Chicago and English in London. The Mishnah stayed in Hebrew, and the Gemara around it was in Aramaic.

words.d: the everyday language of the Middle East in the rabbis' time; the language of most of the Gemara
a rabbi who traveled between the Land of Israel and Babylonia, carrying teachings by memory

look.title: Three Hundred Years of the Gemara
rows: Rav founds the academy at Sura (about)
look.cite: Dates as commonly given by historians of rabbinic literature; most are approximate
look.prompt: About how many years passed between the Mishnah and the Babylonian Talmud? Which came first, the Jerusalem Talmud or the Babylonian?

check.q: How did teachings travel between Babylon and the Land of Israel?
choices: In the memories of rabbis who walked between them
check.why: Travelers like Rav Dimi and Ulla learned teachings by heart and repeated them in the other land.

check.q: What language is most of the Gemara written in?
check.why: The Gemara is mostly Aramaic, the everyday language of the time; the Mishnah is in Hebrew.

check.q: Which was finished first?
check.why: The Jerusalem Talmud was finished around 400 CE, about a century before the Babylonian Talmud.

lessons.title: The Jerusalem Talmud
lessons.mainIdea: The Jerusalem Talmud, finished around 400 CE, is the Gemara of the Land of Israel, though it was made mostly in Tiberias.
reading: The rabbis of the Land of Israel finished their Gemara first, around the year 400. It is called the Jerusalem Talmud, or in Hebrew the *Yerushalmi*. The name is a little surprising. It was not made in Jerusalem. Most of the work was done in Tiberias, in Galilee. The name honors the holy city.

The Yerushalmi is shorter than the Babylonian Talmud. Its arguments are often brief. Historians think the rabbis of the Land of Israel had a hard time under the Roman rulers, who by then were Christian, and the work stopped earlier than it did in Babylon.

The Yerushalmi has Gemara on 39 *tractates* of the Mishnah. A tractate is one book of the Mishnah on one subject. Most of the Yerushalmi's tractates are in the first four orders. It is the main source for the laws of farming in the Land of Israel, which the Babylonian rabbis had less reason to discuss.

words.d: the Jerusalem Talmud, the Gemara of the Land of Israel, finished around 400 CE
one book of the Mishnah on one subject, such as Berakhot on blessings

look.title: A Name and a Place
look.text: A book called the Jerusalem Talmud was written mostly in Tiberias, about 70 miles north of Jerusalem. Readers have given the name two explanations. One: Jerusalem stood for the whole Land of Israel. Two: the name honors the city where the Temple had stood. Either way, the name tells you where the book comes from, not which town.
look.prompt: Can you think of another book, team or place with a name that does not match exactly where it is from?

check.q: Where was most of the Jerusalem Talmud actually made?
check.why: The Yerushalmi was made mostly in Tiberias, in Galilee; its name honors Jerusalem.

check.q: When was the Jerusalem Talmud finished?
check.why: Historians date the Yerushalmi to around 400 CE, about a century before the Babylonian Talmud.

check.q: What is a tractate?
choices: One book of the Mishnah on one subject
check.why: A tractate is one book of the Mishnah about one subject; the Mishnah has 63 of them.

lessons.title: The Babylonian Talmud
lessons.mainIdea: The Babylonian Talmud, finished around 500 CE, is longer than the Yerushalmi and is the Talmud most people study.
reading: The rabbis of Babylonia kept going for another hundred years. Their Gemara is the Babylonian Talmud, or in Hebrew the *Bavli*. Tradition says two teachers at Sura, Rav Ashi and Ravina, gathered and arranged it. Rav Ashi died in 427. The Gemara itself calls them "the end of instruction."

After them came teachers called the *Savoraim*, the "explainers." Between about 500 and 600 they added short notes and smoothed the text. Historians still debate how much of the Bavli was shaped in this time. The book was finished slowly, by many hands, not on one day.

The Bavli has Gemara on 37 tractates. In the standard printing it fills 2,711 leaves, each with two sides. It is long, and its arguments run deep. When people today say "the Talmud" with no other word, they almost always mean the Bavli. It became the main book of Jewish law and study for the next 1,500 years.

words.d: the Babylonian Talmud, finished around 500 CE; the Talmud most people mean when they say "the Talmud"
the "explainers," teachers of about 500 to 600 CE who added notes to the Bavli and smoothed its text

look.title: The End of Instruction
look.text: The Gemara says that Rabbi Judah the Prince and Rabbi Nathan were the end of the Mishnah, and that Rav Ashi and Ravina were the end of instruction. Rashi explains this to mean that after Rav Ashi and Ravina, no one added new rulings to the Talmud in the same way; later teachers explained what was already there.
look.cite: Babylonian Talmud, Bava Metzia 86a, with Rashi's comment, retold in plain words from the William Davidson Talmud (Sefaria, 2017)
look.prompt: Why might a tradition want to name the people who "finished" a book, even if the book was shaped by many hands?

check.q: Which two teachers does tradition name as the arrangers of the Babylonian Talmud?
check.why: Bava Metzia 86a calls Rav Ashi and Ravina "the end of instruction," and tradition sees them as the Bavli's arrangers.

check.q: Who were the Savoraim?
choices: Teachers who added notes to the Bavli after about 500 CE
check.why: The Savoraim, the "explainers," worked on the Bavli's text between about 500 and 600 CE.

check.q: How many leaves does the Babylonian Talmud fill in the standard printing?
check.why: The standard printing of the Bavli has 2,711 leaves, each with two sides; 63 is the number of Mishnah tractates.

lessons.title: Why Two, and Which One?
lessons.mainIdea: Both Talmuds discuss the same Mishnah, but the Bavli became the main one because the Babylonian community and its later teachers spread it.
reading: Why are there two Talmuds? Because there were two centers, each with its own rabbis, questions and language. Both start from the same Mishnah. Often they reach the same answer by different roads. Sometimes they disagree. Readers who compare them can see how one question looked from two places.

The Bavli became the main Talmud for a simple reason. The Jewish community of Babylonia stayed strong for centuries. After the Talmud, its academies were led by teachers called the *Geonim*. From about 600 to 1000 they answered questions sent from Jewish communities everywhere, and their answers followed the Bavli.

So the Bavli became the base of *halakhah*, Jewish law as the rabbis develop it. The Yerushalmi was studied less, but never forgotten. Today Orthodox, Conservative and Reform scholars all study both, and university scholars compare them to see how the text grew. Both are open to anyone who wants to read.

words.d: the heads of the Babylonian academies from about 600 to 1000 CE, who spread the Bavli by answering questions from far away
Jewish law as the rabbis develop it from the Torah, the Mishnah and the Talmud

look.title: Counting the Tractates
rows: Tractates with Gemara in the Jerusalem Talmud
Tractates with Gemara in the Babylonian Talmud
look.cite: Common counts for the standard printed editions; scholars count a few tractates differently
look.prompt: The Yerushalmi covers more tractates than the Bavli, yet the Bavli is much longer. How can both be true?

check.q: Why did the Bavli become the main Talmud?
choices: The Babylonian community stayed strong and its Geonim spread it
It was the only Talmud ever written
check.why: The academies of Babylonia lasted for centuries, and the Geonim answered questions from everywhere using the Bavli.

check.q: What does halakhah mean?
choices: Jewish law as the rabbis develop it
check.why: Halakhah is Jewish law as developed from the Torah, the Mishnah and the Talmud; stories are aggadah.

check.q: What do the two Talmuds have in common?
choices: The same Mishnah at their center
check.why: Both Talmuds are Gemara on the same Mishnah, made in two different lands by different rabbis.

review.q: Roughly how many years did the rabbis of the Gemara discuss the Mishnah?
review.why: The amoraim worked from about 200 to about 500 CE, roughly three hundred years.

review.q: Which two lands were the homes of the Gemara?
choices: The Land of Israel and Babylonia
review.why: The Gemara was made in the Land of Israel, especially Galilee, and in Babylonia, today's Iraq.

review.q: What language is the Mishnah written in, and what language is most of the Gemara?
choices: Mishnah in Hebrew, Gemara mostly in Aramaic
Mishnah in Greek, Gemara in Hebrew
review.why: The Mishnah is in Hebrew; the Gemara around it is mostly in Aramaic, the everyday language of the time.

review.q: Which two academies were the great schools of Babylonia?
review.why: Sura, founded by Rav, and Pumbedita, which rose after Nehardea fell, were Babylonia's two great academies.

review.q: Which Talmud is longer and more widely studied?
review.why: The Bavli is much longer and became the main book of Jewish law and study.

review.q: What does the Gemara call Rav Ashi and Ravina?
choices: The men of the Great Assembly
review.why: Bava Metzia 86a names Rav Ashi and Ravina as "the end of instruction," and tradition sees them as the Bavli's arrangers.

review.q: Who was the leader of the Jewish community in Babylonia under the Persian kings?
review.why: The Exilarch, "head of the exile," led the community and spoke for it at the Persian court.

review.q: A page of Gemara shows the question, the proof, the objection and the reply. What does this tell you about the rabbis?
choices: They only cared about the final answer
They kept the whole argument, including views that lost
review.why: The Gemara keeps every step and every side of an argument, so a reader can follow the path and hear the minority too.
